In [[mathematics]], the '''Artin&ndash;Rees lemma''' is a basic result about [[module (mathematics)|module]]s over a [[Noetherian ring]], along with results such as the [[Hilbert basis theorem]]. It was proved in the 1950s in independent works by the [[mathematician]]s [[Emil Artin]] and [[David Rees (mathematician)|David Rees]];<ref>{{harvnb|Rees|1956|loc=Lemma 1}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Sharp|2015|loc=Section 7, Lemma 7.2, Page 10}}</ref> a special case was known to [[Oscar Zariski]] prior to their work.

An intuitive characterization of the lemma involves the notion that a submodule ''N'' of a module ''M'' over some ring ''A'' with specified ideal ''I'' holds ''a priori'' two topologies: one induced by the topology on ''M,'' and the other when considered with the ''I-adic'' topology over ''A.'' Then Artin-Rees dictates that these topologies actually coincide, at least when ''A'' is Noetherian and ''M'' finitely-generated.

One consequence of the lemma is the [[Krull intersection theorem]]. The result is also used to prove the exactness property of [[completion (ring theory)|completion]].<ref>{{harvnb|Atiyah|MacDonald|1969|loc=pp. 107–109}}</ref> The lemma also plays a key role in the study of [[ℓ-adic sheaf|ℓ-adic sheaves]].

==Statement ==
Let ''I'' be an [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] in a [[Noetherian ring]] ''R''; let ''M'' be a [[finitely generated module|finitely generated ''R''-module]] and let ''N'' a submodule of ''M''. Then there exists an integer ''k''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;1 so that, for ''n''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;''k'',

:<math>I^{n} M \cap N = I^{n - k} (I^{k} M \cap N).</math>

== Proof ==
The lemma immediately follows from the fact that ''R'' is Noetherian once necessary notions and notations are set up.<ref>{{harvnb|Eisenbud|1995|loc=Lemma 5.1}}</ref>

For any ring ''R'' and an ideal ''I'' in ''R'', we set <math display="inline">B_I R = \bigoplus_{n=0}^\infty I^n</math> (''B'' for blow-up.) We say a decreasing sequence of submodules <math>M = M_0 \supset M_1 \supset M_2 \supset \cdots</math> is an ''I''-filtration if <math>I M_n \subset M_{n+1}</math>; moreover, it is stable if <math>I M_n = M_{n+1}</math> for sufficiently large ''n''. If ''M'' is given an ''I''-filtration, we set <math display="inline">B_I M = \bigoplus_{n=0}^\infty M_n</math>; it is a [[graded module]] over <math>B_I R</math>.

Now, let ''M'' be a ''R''-module with the ''I''-filtration <math>M_i</math> by finitely generated ''R''-modules. We make an observation
:<math>B_I M</math> is a finitely generated module over <math>B_I R</math> if and only if the filtration is ''I''-stable.
Indeed, if the filtration is ''I''-stable, then <math>B_I M</math> is generated by the first <math>k+1</math> terms <math>M_0, \dots, M_k</math> and those terms are finitely generated; thus, <math>B_I M</math> is finitely generated. Conversely, if it is finitely generated, then it is generated by <math display="inline">\bigoplus_{j=0}^k M_j</math> for some <math>k \ge 0</math>. Then, for <math>n > k</math>, each ''f'' in <math>M_n</math> can be written as
<math display="block">f = \sum a_{j} g_{j}, \quad a_{j} \in I^{n-j}</math>
with <math>g_{j}</math> in <math>M_j, j \le k</math>. That is, <math>f \in I^{n-k} M_k</math>.

We can now prove the lemma, assuming ''R'' is Noetherian. Let <math>M_n = I^n M</math>. Then <math>M_n</math> are an ''I''-stable filtration. Thus, by the observation, <math>B_I M</math> is finitely generated over <math>B_I R</math>. But <math>B_I R \simeq R[It]</math> is a Noetherian ring since ''R'' is. (The ring <math>R[It]</math> is called the [[Rees algebra]].) Thus, <math>B_I M</math> is a Noetherian module and any submodule is finitely generated over <math>B_I R</math>; in particular, <math>B_I N</math> is finitely generated when ''N'' is given the induced filtration; i.e., <math>N_n = M_n \cap N</math>. Then the induced filtration is ''I''-stable again by the observation.

== Krull's intersection theorem ==
Besides the use in completion of a ring, a typical application of the lemma is the proof of the Krull's intersection theorem, which says: <math display="inline">\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty I^n = 0</math> for a proper ideal ''I'' in a commutative Noetherian ring that is either a [[local ring]] or an [[integral domain]]. By the lemma applied to the intersection <math>N</math>, we find ''k'' such that for <math>n \ge k</math>,
<math display="block">I^{n} \cap N = I^{n - k} (I^{k} \cap N).</math>
Taking <math>n = k+1</math>, this means <math>I^{k+1}\cap N = I(I^{k}\cap N)</math> or <math>N = IN</math>. Thus, if ''A'' is local, <math>N = 0</math> by [[Nakayama's lemma]]. If ''A'' is an integral domain, then one uses the determinant trick<ref>{{harvnb|Atiyah|MacDonald|1969|loc=Proposition 2.4}}</ref> (that is, a variant of the [[Cayley–Hamilton theorem]] that yields [[Nakayama's lemma]]):

{{math theorem | math_statement = Let ''u'' be an [[endomorphism]] of an ''A''-module ''N'' generated by ''n'' elements and ''I'' an ideal of ''A'' such that <math>u(N) \subset IN</math>. Then there is a relation: <math display="block">u^n + a_1 u^{n-1} + \cdots  + a_{n-1} u + a_n = 0, \, a_i \in I^i.</math>}}

In the setup here, take ''u'' to be the identity operator on ''N''; that will yield a nonzero element ''x'' in ''A'' such that <math>x N = 0</math>, which implies <math>N = 0</math>, as <math>x</math> is a nonzerodivisor.

For both a local ring and an integral domain, the "Noetherian" cannot be dropped from the assumption: for the local ring case, see [[local ring#Commutative case]]. For the integral domain case, take <math>A</math> to be the [[ring of algebraic integers]] (i.e., the integral closure of <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> in <math>\mathbb{C}</math>). If <math>\mathfrak p</math> is a prime ideal of ''A'', then we have: <math>\mathfrak{p}^n = \mathfrak{p}</math> for every integer <math>n > 0</math>. Indeed, if <math>y \in \mathfrak p</math>, then <math>y = \alpha^n</math> for some complex number <math>\alpha</math>. Now, <math>\alpha</math> is integral over <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>; thus in <math>A</math> and then in <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>, proving the claim.

Both the cases of the Noetherian ring being local and the Noetherian ring being an integral domain are consequences of a more general version of Krull's intersection theorem, which is also a consequence of the Artin–Rees and Nakayama lemmata:<ref>{{harvnb|Atiyah|MacDonald|1969|loc=Theorem 10.17}}</ref>

{{math theorem
| math_statement = Let ''I'' be an ideal of commutative Noetherian ring ''A'' and ''M'' be a finitely generated ''A''-module.  Set <math>N:=\textstyle\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} I^n M.</math> Then there exists <math>x\in 1+I</math> such that ''x'' annihilates ''N''.
| name = Theorem (Krull Intersection)
}}
